The City of Toledo, in which the Ohio Supreme Court first recognized the authority of a municipality to levy and collect municipal income taxes under rule, and also established the due process standard for challenges to those taxes. The Angle court answered two questions. The first was whether a municipality had any authority whatsoever to tax the income of non-residents. The court answered that question by holding that such authority exists, pursuant to the Home Rule Amendment, and subject to such limitations that the legislature may impose under Article 18.

There, the Angle Court borrowed from the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in the state of Wisconsin v. J.C. Penney Company to adopt a fiscal relationship test for municipal income tax, which requires that the taxpayer a fiscal relation to the protections, opportunities, and benefits given. The Ohio Supreme Court has reaffirmed this test repeatedly. In 1961, in the case of McConnell v. City of Columbus, the court upheld the city's income tax against an Ohio resident who was not a Columbus resident by applying Angle's fiscal relation test, reasoning that even though the employee worked for an arm of the state of Ohio and on state property, he still performed his work within the city of Columbus. And that was key. Subsequently, in Thompson v. The City of Cincinnati, the court once again reaffirmed that there are two instances in which the city may tax wages. Quote, a municipality may tax wages realized within that municipality by a non-resident, citing Angle, and may tax the wages of a resident realized from a source outside the municipality. Recently, a unanimous Ohio Supreme Court summarized its 72 years of consistent precedent in Hillenmeyer v. Cleveland Board of Review. In that case, the court found that beyond in-person taxing over residents, local authorities may tax non-residents only if theirs is the jurisdiction.
